00-index.title: IBM Arteriole Wall Simulation — Report (Blood_vessel_v2)
00-index.content:
2D Immersed Boundary Simulation of an Arteriole Wall


                  
                  Abstract 
                  
                

We model a straight segment of a small cerebral artery (D_0 = 150\ \mum, L = 1.5 mm) as two elastic walls immersed in blood, using a 2D penalty immersed boundary method with an FFT-based Navier–Stokes solver in physical units (\nu = 3.3\times10^{-6} m²/s). The walls are held by uniform tethers (stiff along the wall, weak across it) and membrane springs; a myogenic passive-stress law is implemented but currently switched off. Flow is driven by a uniform, time-modulated body force that stands in for a pulsatile pressure gradient (u_\max \approx 2.5 mm/s, Re \approx 0.11, Womersley \alpha\approx0.1).
The project goal at this stage is a parameter set for which the wall oscillates regularly without numerical blow-up. Starting from a stable March 2026 configuration (non-physical code units), we derived a load-to-stiffness mapping to physical scale (K_\text{phys} = 9.36\times10^5\,K_\text{March}). The mapped parameters give periodic wall motion (diameter oscillation ≈ 2 %) and reproduce plane Poiseuille flow to within 7 %, but longer runs reveal a compressive collapse of the wall: the mean shear drags the wall downstream against its pinned ends. An anisotropic tether (strong axially, weak radially) removes the collapse and leaves the wall free to move radially; with the present uniform drive, however, nothing loads the wall radially and the closed periodic lumen conserves its area, so the wall barely moves. The next step is a pressure-controlled source/sink (as in Arthurs et al., 1998) to pressurize the lumen, so that dilation and constriction can be studied through the myogenic stress.


Contents

01 Introduction — motivation, scope, goal
02 IBM Formulation — governing equations, discrete delta, penalty IB, fluid solver, time stepping
03 Problem Setup — 2D periodic channel, unit system, Poiseuille baseline, dimensionless numbers
04 Boundary Configuration — wall discretization, target points, tether profile
05 Forces — tether, spring, myogenic (Eq. 18), driving force
06 Code Implementation — files, switches, outputs, environment
06 Parameters — parameter discussion, March → physical mapping, parameter table
07 Experiments — all runs from 2026-03 to 2026-10, baseline result
08 References

01-introduction.title: 01 Introduction
01-introduction.content:
1. Introduction
← 00 Index | Next: 02 IBM Formulation
1.1 Motivation
Cerebral blood flow is regulated by vasomotor tone — the active dilation and constriction of arterial walls in response to mechanical and biochemical signals. Two mechanisms dominate in small arteries and arterioles:

the myogenic response: smooth muscle contracts when the transmural pressure rises, keeping flow roughly constant;
nitric-oxide (NO) mediated vasodilation: NO released by endothelial cells relaxes the smooth muscle and dilates the vessel.

When this regulation fails (endothelial dysfunction, vasospasm, atherosclerosis) the consequences include stroke and cognitive decline. How vasomotor tone interacts with pulsatile blood flow is computationally under-explored: many models treat the wall as rigid or reduce the vessel to 1D, which misses wall shear-stress asymmetry and secondary flow structures.
Vessel-wall motion is a fluid–structure interaction (FSI) problem — the wall deforms under flow loads, and its motion changes the flow — which motivates a method that couples a moving elastic boundary to a viscous fluid.
1.2 Why the immersed boundary method

The fluid lives on a fixed Cartesian (Eulerian) grid and the wall is a set of moving Lagrangian points; the two communicate through a smoothed delta function. No body-fitted remeshing is needed as the wall deforms (Peskin, 1972; Peskin, 2002).
IBM has been used for arteriolar flow with a myogenic wall model (Arthurs et al., 1998) — the closest prior work to this project.
A penalty IB variant (ghost/target points tied to the boundary by stiff springs) lets us pin the vessel ends and later prescribe wall motion (e.g. NO-driven dilation) through the target points.

02-ibm-formulation.title: 02 IBM Formulation
02-ibm-formulation.content:
2. Immersed Boundary Method — Formulation
← 01 Introduction | Next: 03 Problem Setup


                  
                  Source 
                  
                

Adapted from my notes Notes/IMB_Introduction/Section_1.tex and Notes/Penalty_Immersed_Boundary/section2.tex, and Peskin’s lectures (08 References). Implementation details refer to MATLAB/Blood_vessel_v2/helpers/.


2.1 Continuous formulation
Incompressible Navier–Stokes for the fluid on \Omega:
\rho\left(\frac{\partial \mathbf u}{\partial t}+\mathbf u\cdot\nabla\mathbf u\right)=-\nabla p+\mu\nabla^2\mathbf u+\mathbf f,\qquad \nabla\cdot\mathbf u=0
Fluid–structure coupling through the Dirac delta functions
\mathbf f(\mathbf x,t)=\int_\Gamma \mathbf F(s,t)\,\delta\big(\mathbf x-\mathbf X(s,t)\big)\,ds,
\qquad
\frac{\partial \mathbf X}{\partial t}(s,t)=\int_\Omega \mathbf u(\mathbf x,t)\,\delta\big(\mathbf x-\mathbf X(s,t)\big)\,d\mathbf x

\mathbf X(s,t) is the wall position (Lagrangian), \mathbf F(s,t): force density on the wall, \mathbf f: force density on the fluid.
The boundary is massless and moves with the local fluid velocity (no-slip); all its elastic forces are transmitted to the fluid.

2.2 Discretization
Discrete delta function
\delta_h(\mathbf x)=\frac{1}{\Delta x\,\Delta y}\,\phi\!\left(\frac{x}{\Delta x}\right)\phi\!\left(\frac{y}{\Delta y}\right)
Here we use the Peskin 4-point kernel functions which is basically a discretized delta function :
\phi(r)=\begin{cases}
\dfrac{1}{8}\left(3-2|r|+\sqrt{1+4|r|-4r^2}\right), & |r|\le 1\\[3pt]
\dfrac{1}{8}\left(5-2|r|-\sqrt{-7+12|r|-4r^2}\right), & 1\le|r|\le 2\\[3pt]
0, & |r|\ge 2
\end{cases}

Support: 4×4 grid points per Lagrangian point → the wall is smeared over ≈ 2 grid cells (consequence: 09 Discussion > Effective channel width).

Spreading and interpolation
\mathbf f_{ij}=\sum_k \mathbf F_k\,\delta_h(\mathbf x_{ij}-\mathbf X_k)\,\Delta s,
\qquad
\mathbf U_k=\sum_{ij}\mathbf u_{ij}\,\delta_h(\mathbf x_{ij}-\mathbf X_k)\,\Delta x\,\Delta y

\Delta s is the variable dtheta (see 09 Discussion > dtheta vs node spacing).
In this step, because the force is described on the Lagrange coordinate to match the structure boundaries, we need to spread it to Euclidian coordinate to describes it in fluid solver.

2.3 Penalty immersed boundary (pIB)

Two sets of points: massless boundary points \mathbf X (move with the fluid) and ghost/target points \mathbf Y (carry mass, infinite mass if needed, do not touch the fluid), linked by a stiff spring:

\mathbf F=K\,(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X)

In v2, \mathbf Y is fixed at the initial wall position (never updated) → the penalty spring acts as a tether to fixed anchors, not a full massive pIB. Moving \mathbf Y is the planned hook for prescribed dilation (NO). Details: 04 Boundary Configuration, 05 Forces > 5.1 Tether (penalty) force.

2.4 Fluid solver
The domain is doubly periodic, so all linear operators are diagonalized by the discrete Fourier transform (navier_stokes_solver_pIB.m, operators precomputed in init_a_circ.m, init_b.m).
Spatial operators (second-order central differences):

Central difference D^0:

(D^0_x g)_{ij}=\frac{g_{i+1,j}-g_{i-1,j}}{2\Delta x}

Skew-symmetric advection (skew_symmetric_advection.m, sk_operator.m), an energy-neutral discretization of \mathbf u\cdot\nabla g:

S(\mathbf u)\,g=\tfrac12\,\mathbf u\cdot D^0 g+\tfrac12\,D^0\!\cdot(\mathbf u\,g)

5-point Laplacian L_h (laplacian_tube.m), with Fourier symbol

\hat L=-\frac{4}{\Delta x^2}\left[\sin^2\!\frac{\pi m_1}{N_x}+\sin^2\!\frac{\pi m_2}{N_y}\right]

Discrete projection onto divergence-free fields, where \hat{\mathbf s} is the Fourier symbol of D^0:

\hat P = I-\frac{\hat{\mathbf s}\,\hat{\mathbf s}^{\mathsf T}}{|\hat{\mathbf s}|^2},\qquad
\hat{\mathbf s}=\Big(\sin\frac{2\pi m_1}{N_x},\ \sin\frac{2\pi m_2}{N_y}\Big)
Time step (Peskin’s two-stage scheme; \mathbf f is the force at \mathbf X^{n+1/2}):
\mathbf u^{n+1/2}=\hat P\Big(I-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\nu L_h\Big)^{-1}\Big[\mathbf u^n-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}S(\mathbf u^n)\mathbf u^n+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\mathbf f\Big]
\mathbf u^{n+1}=\hat P\Big(I-\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\nu L_h\Big)^{-1}\Big[\mathbf u^n-\Delta t\,S(\mathbf u^{n+1/2})\mathbf u^{n+1/2}+\tfrac{\Delta t}{2}\nu L_h\mathbf u^n+\Delta t\,\mathbf f\Big]

Stage 1 is a backward-Euler half step, stage 2 is Crank–Nicolson for viscosity with midpoint advection → second order in time.
Since 2026-06-15 the implicit factor uses the full Laplacian symbol (previously only the own-direction part), so the viscous term is unconditionally stable; \Delta t is limited by the advective CFL and by the wall stiffness only.
Pressure is recovered from the divergence of the stage-2 right-hand side (\hat p=\hat{\mathbf b}\cdot\hat{\mathbf w}, init_b.m).
Blow-up detector: the solver stops with an error if \mathbf u contains NaN/Inf.
Note: the Laplacian and the CN factor use \Delta x in both directions; with \Delta x=5.859, \Delta y=5.882 µm the mismatch is 0.4 %.

2.5 Time stepping of the full IB system (main.m)
flowchart LR
  A["X^n, u^n"] --> B["X^{n+1/2} = X^n + Δt/2 · U(u^n, X^n)"]
  B --> C["F = F_tether(X^{n+1/2}) + F_spring(X^n) + F_myo(X^n)"]
  C --> D["f = S[F] at X^{n+1/2} + f_drive(t)"]
  D --> E["NS solve (2.4) → u^{n+1}"]
  E --> F["X^{n+1} = X^n + Δt · U(u^{n+1}, X^{n+1/2})"]


The tether force is evaluated at the half-step position, while the spring and myogenic forces currently use \mathbf X^n (main.m, force block). This is first-order in those terms; harmless for the present small deformations, but worth unifying.

03-problem-setup.title: 03 Problem Setup
03-problem-setup.content:
3. Problem Setup
← 02 IBM Formulation | Next: 04 Boundary Configuration
3.1 Physical sc03 Problem Setupenario

A straight segment of a small cerebral artery / large arteriole: rest diameter D_0 = 150\ \mum, length L_x = 1.5 mm.
2D planar model: two elastic walls (top, bottom) immersed in fluid; fluid fills both the lumen and the region outside the vessel.
Blood is modelled as a Newtonian fluid with its real kinematic viscosity.
Flow is driven by a uniform body force inside the lumen, modulated in time to mimic a pulsatile pressure gradient (05 Forces > 5.4 Driving force).

 y=500 ┌──────────────────────────────────────────────┐   periodic in y
       │                 exterior fluid                │
 y=325 │●━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ top wall ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━●│  ● strongly tethered ends
       │      →  →  →   f = G·g(t) e_x (lumen only)  →  │
 y=175 │●━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━━ bottom wall ━━━━━━━━━━━━━━●│
       │                 exterior fluid                │
 y=0   └──────────────────────────────────────────────┘
       x=0                                       x=1500 µm   periodic in x

3.2 Domain and grid

Domain [0,L_x]\times[0,L_y] = 1500\times 500\ \mum, periodic in x and y.
Grid N_x\times N_y = 256\times 85, \Delta x = 5.859 µm, \Delta y = 5.882 µm → 25 grid rows across the lumen.
Each wall spans the whole periodic length, so the lumen is a closed periodic channel (consequence: 09 Discussion > Lumen area is conserved).

3.3 Unit system


                  
                  Important
                  
                

Length in µm, time in s, density normalized out (\rho=1).

\nu [µm²/s] — kinematic viscosity
body force G, stiffnesses K [µm/s²] — per unit density
stress \sigma, pressure p [µm²/s²] — per unit density



3.4 Baseline: plane Poiseuille flow
Steady flow between rigid plates a distance H apart, driven by a uniform gradient G:
u(y)=\frac{G}{2\nu}\,(y-y_b)(y_t-y),\qquad u_{\max}=\frac{G H^2}{8\nu},\qquad \bar u=\tfrac{2}{3}u_{\max},\qquad \tau_w=\frac{G H}{2}
With G = 2.933\times10^6 µm/s², H = D_0: u_{\max}=2.5 mm/s, wall shear stress \tau_w\approx2.2\times10^8 µm²/s² (\approx0.23 Pa).
The uniform body force is exactly the periodic-domain stand-in for a mean pressure gradient: the physical pressure is p_\text{phys}(x)=p_\text{periodic}(x)-\rho G x.
3.5 Dimensionless numbers

04-boundary-configuration.title: 04 Boundary Configuration
04-boundary-configuration.content:
4. Boundary Configuration
← 03 Problem Setup | Next: 05 Forces
4.1 Wall discretization

Two walls (top, bottom), each an open chain of N_b = 512 Lagrangian points spanning the full domain length (200 before 2026-10-14).
Initial positions:

X^{\text{top}}_k=\Big(x_k,\ \tfrac{L_y}{2}+\tfrac{D_0}{2}\Big),\quad
X^{\text{bot}}_k=\Big(x_k,\ \tfrac{L_y}{2}-\tfrac{D_0}{2}\Big),\quad
x_k=\frac{k\,L_x}{N_b-1},\ k=0,\dots,N_b-1

Nodes k=0 and k=N_b-1 sit at x=0 and x=L_x, which coincide under periodicity.

4.2 Ghost / target points
The ghost point is a special modification in Immersed boundary method to represent a restoring force that drag the drifted boundary point to it’s initial condition. In order to simulate a solid.

\mathbf Y^{\text{top}}=\mathbf X^{\text{top}}(t=0), \mathbf Y^{\text{bot}}=\mathbf X^{\text{bot}}(t=0), fixed in time.
Every wall point is tethered to its own target point (see 05 Forces > 5.1 Tether (penalty) force).

4.3 Tether stiffness (uniform, anisotropic)
Every wall node is tied to its own target point with separate stiffnesses along the wall (x) and across it (y). Both stiffnesses are the same at every node (no extra anchoring at the ends):
F^{\text{tet}}_{k,x}=K_x\,(Y_{k,x}-X_{k,x}),\qquad
F^{\text{tet}}_{k,y}=K_y\,(Y_{k,y}-X_{k,y})























DirectionCode variableValue (µm/s²)Rolex (axial, along the wall)K_wall_x2.34\times10^9 ("K_\text{tar}" in 07 Experiments)strong: holds the wall against the mean wall shear, so it does not drift downstreamy (radial, across the wall)K_wall_y9.36\times10^5weak: the radial position is left to the fluid pressure, the springs and the myogenic stress

The axial tether is uniform so that the shear moves every node by the same amount: the wall shifts as a whole instead of being compressed against fixed ends.
The radial tether is uniform because the periodic domain stands for an infinitely long vessel, which must dilate uniformly. Stiff radial anchoring at the ends created a “pinch” that tore the wall once the lumen was pressurized (2026-10-13).
The code still contains an older exponential end-anchoring formula (tether_profile, K_tar, decay_len), but with the current values it has no effect in main.m: the axial profile is clipped to K_wall_x everywhere (K_tar_vec_x = 2.34e9 at all nodes), and the radial profile is set to K_wall_y directly.

Why anisotropic. With the former isotropic floor K_\text{wall}=9.36\times10^6 in both directions:

the mean wall shear dragged the wall interior ≈ 37 µm downstream while the ends stayed fixed, putting the downstream half under ≈ 9 % compression; the spring chain (no bending stiffness) then collapsed locally after ≈ 22 s (a=0.2) or ≈ 8 s (a=0.6) — see 08a Earlier Experiments > A.8 Long-run compressive collapse (isotropic tether);
the same radial tether pulled any outward bulge back, so the radial balance was set by the tether rather than by pressure vs. myogenic stress.

Physically, the axial anchoring stands for the perivascular tissue that holds a vessel in place lengthwise, while the radial direction must stay free for dilation/constriction.


                  
                  Experiment scripts 
                  
                

The older experiment_*.m scripts still use the legacy isotropic, exponentially decaying profile K_tar_vec (ends K_tar = 2.34e8, interior K_wall = 9.36e6) in their own copy of the time loop. main.m does not use it.


4.4 Node pairing for the myogenic force

Top node k is paired with bottom node k (same index, same initial x).
Local “diameter” r_k=|y^{\text{top}}_k-y^{\text{bot}}_k|. Valid while the walls stay roughly horizontal and do not slide relative to each other.

05-forces.title: 05 Forces
05-forces.content:
5. Forces in the System
← 04 Boundary Configuration | Next: 06 Code Implementation
Overview






















































#ForceActs onFormulaStatus1Tether (penalty)wall nodes (Lagrangian)\mathrm{diag}(K_x,K_y)(\mathbf Y_k-\mathbf X_k)on2Spring (membrane tension)wall nodesHooke along each wallon3Myogenic passive stress (Eq. 18)wall nodes, y onlytwo-branch law, per unit wall lengthon (calibrated, 2026-10-13)4Driving body forcefluid (Eulerian), horizontal onlyG\,g(t)\,\mathbf e_xon (use_flow_drive = true; stable with N_b=512, 2026-10-14)5Pressure-controlled source/sinkfluid (mass source, not a force)\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf u=q(t)(w_\text{in}-w_\text{out})on — 5.5 Lumen pressurization (source/sink)(6)Bending stiffnesswall nodes-K_b\,\Delta^4\mathbf X/\Delta s_0^4implemented, off
Forces 1–3 are summed and spread to the grid; force 4 is added directly on the grid; item 5 modifies the incompressibility constraint:
\mathbf f = \mathcal S\big[\mathbf F_\text{tet}+\mathbf F_\text{spr}+\mathbf F_\text{myo}\big] + \mathbf f_\text{drive}(t),\qquad \nabla\!\cdot\mathbf u = s(\mathbf x,t)
The force \mathbf{f} is the force appeared in the fluid solver.
5.1 Tether (penalty) force
Anisotropic, with a separate stiffness along (x) and across (y) the wall, the same at every node:
\mathbf F^{\text{tet}}_k = \begin{pmatrix} K_x\,(Y_{k,x}-X_{k,x})\\[2pt] K_y\,(Y_{k,y}-X_{k,y})\end{pmatrix},\qquad K_x=2.34\times10^9,\quad K_y=9.36\times10^5\ \text{µm/s}^2

Details and history: 04 Boundary Configuration > 4.3 Tether stiffness (uniform, anisotropic).
Role: holds the wall axially against the mean wall shear (no downstream drift, no compressive collapse; the strong axial anchoring also delays pressure-induced buckling), while leaving it nearly free radially, where pressure, springs and myogenic stress set the diameter.
Code (main.m):

F_penalty_top(:, 1) = K_tar_vec_x' .* (Y_top(:, 1) - X_half_top(:, 1));
F_penalty_top(:, 2) = K_tar_vec_y' .* (Y_top(:, 2) - X_half_top(:, 2));
5.2 Spring (membrane) force
For segment k connecting nodes k\to k+1 on the same wall:
T_k = K_\text{mem}\big(|\mathbf X_{k+1}-\mathbf X_k|-\Delta s_0\big),\qquad
\boldsymbol\tau_k=\frac{\mathbf X_{k+1}-\mathbf X_k}{|\mathbf X_{k+1}-\mathbf X_k|}
\mathbf F^{\text{spr}}_k \mathrel{+}= T_k\boldsymbol\tau_k,\qquad \mathbf F^{\text{spr}}_{k+1}\mathrel{-}= T_k\boldsymbol\tau_k

Open chain (no wrap-around).
🟡**No pre-tension**: rest length = initial spacing, so a straight wall carries zero tension and has zero transverse stiffness to first order. The spring only resists axial stretching/compression.

5.3 Myogenic force (Michele et al. (2006), Eq. 18)
\sigma_p(r)=\begin{cases}
\sigma_{p0}\left(e^{k_p(r-r_0)}-1\right), & r\ge r_0\\[4pt]
\sigma_{p0}\,k_p\left(1-\left(\dfrac{r^2}{r_0^2}\right)^{-3/2}\right), & r<r_0
\end{cases}
\qquad
F^{\text{myo,top}}_{k,y}=-\sigma_p(r_k),\quad F^{\text{myo,bot}}_{k,y}=+\sigma_p(r_k)

r_k = local diameter, r_0=D_0. \sigma_p>0 is contractile (walls pulled toward the centerline); \sigma_p<0 pushes them apart.
Physical meaning: passive (elastic) stress of the smooth-muscle wall that stiffens exponentially with stretch — the stress that balances transmural pressure in a real vessel.
Enabled since 2026-10-13 to balance the transmural pressure of the pressurized lumen.

Per unit wall length. \sigma_p is a stress, so each node carries the wall length it represents, \ell_k=\tfrac12(L_{k-1}+L_k):
F^{\text{myo,top}}_{k,y}=-\sigma_p(r_k)\,\frac{\ell_k}{\Delta s_0},\qquad F^{\text{myo,bot}}_{k,y}=+\sigma_p(r_k)\,\frac{\ell_k}{\Delta s_0}
(at the two coincident end nodes \ell_k is half a segment, so the shared point is not counted twice).
Calibration. At equilibrium the spread myogenic force per unit length balances the transmural pressure, \sigma_p(r_\text{eq})\,\Delta s/\Delta s_0=P_\text{set}. Choosing the target dilation r_\text{eq}-r_0=\varepsilon D_0 gives
\sigma_{p0}=\frac{P_\text{set}\,\Delta s_0/\Delta s}{e^{k_p\varepsilon D_0}-1}
\;\approx 3.0\times10^{8}\ \mu\text{m}^2/\text{s}^2\quad(P_\text{set}=2\ \text{Pa},\ \varepsilon=0.2,\ k_p=0.1)
Stimulation. The stress scale is multiplied by a user-defined activation, \sigma_{p0}\,a_\text{myo}(t) (myo_activation). For a step change a_\text{myo}=a the new equilibrium is
\frac{D_\text{eq}}{D_0}=1+\frac{1}{k_pD_0}\ln\!\Big(1+\frac{e^{k_p\varepsilon D_0}-1}{a}\Big)
→ a=2 (stronger smooth-muscle tone): D/D_0=1.157; a=0.5 (relaxation, e.g. NO): D/D_0=1.245.
For comparison — Arthurs et al. (1998), Eq. 60 (Voigt viscoelastic model, used in v3 and in v2 before May 2026):
M(s,t)=K_M\,\frac{D(s,t)}{D_0}+\gamma\,\frac{\partial_t D(s,t)}{D_0}
5.4 Driving force
\mathbf f_\text{drive}(\mathbf x,t)=G\;g(t)\;\mathbf e_x\qquad\text{for every grid point strictly inside the lumen } (y_b<y<y_t),
zero outside the vessel. Here the function g(t) is either a constant or a time oscilating function + a constant.

Time-modulation switch (initialize.m):

use_osc_drive = false → steady drive, g\equiv1;
use_osc_drive = true → g(t)= drive_profile(t), any user-supplied function handle. Default: g(t)=1+a\sin(2\pi t/T) with a=0.2, T=1 s (60 bpm; the drive never reverses for a<1).



5.5 Lumen pressurization (source/sink)
Following Arthurs et al. (1998, Eqs. 5–9). A closed periodic lumen conserves its area, so it cannot inflate unless fluid can enter it. A fluid source inside the lumen and a matching sink in the exterior exchange fluid at a pressure-controlled rate:
\nabla\!\cdot\mathbf u = s(\mathbf x,t)=q(t)\,\big(w_\text{in}(\mathbf x)-w_\text{out}(\mathbf x)\big),\qquad
q(t)=\frac{P_\text{set}-P_\text{lumen}(t)}{R_\text{src}},\qquad
P_\text{lumen}=\sum_{ij}p_{ij}\,(w_\text{in}-w_\text{out})_{ij}\,\Delta x\Delta y

w_\text{in}: uniform over the rows |y-L_y/2|<37.5 µm (inside the lumen); w_\text{out}: uniform over the rows within 60 µm of y=0 (exterior). Each is normalized to \sum w\,\Delta x\Delta y=1, so the total source is zero, as a periodic field requires.
Like a short tube of resistance R_\text{src} connecting the lumen to a reservoir at P_\text{set}: fluid flows in while P_\text{lumen}<P_\text{set} and back out if the wall squeezes the lumen (P_\text{lumen}>P_\text{set}). At equilibrium q=0 and the transmural pressure equals P_\text{set}; the lumen area is free to change.
P_\text{lumen} is taken from the previous step’s pressure (explicit update).


Where fluid is added and removed. The source band sits on the lumen centerline, the sink band in the exterior next to y=0 (the same band also appears at the top because the domain is periodic in y). Fluid added in the lumen can only leave by pushing the walls outward; the exterior fluid they displace flows to the sink.

06-parameters.title: 06 Parameters
06-parameters.content:
7. Parameters
← 06 Code Implementation | Next: 07 Experiments
7.1 Parameter groups

Numerical — \Delta t, T_\max, N_x, N_y, N_b. Here N_b is the number of lagrangian point on the boundary.
Fluid — \nu: physical (blood).
Geometry — L_x, L_y, D_0: physical scale of a small cerebral artery.
Wall mechanics — K_{\text{wall},x}, K_{\text{wall},y}, K_\text{mem}: numerical stiffnesses, first obtained by mapping a stable earlier configuration (7.3 March → physical mapping) and then set by the parameter study (07 Experiments > 8.2 Stable parameter range for K_mem, K_tar and σ_p0); not yet derived from wall modulus/thickness.
Myogenic — \sigma_{p0}, k_p, r_0.
Drive — G, g(t) (T, a): chosen for a target peak speed and a heart-rate-like period.

8.1 Configuration and diagnostics
Common set-up

8.2 Stable parameter range for K_mem, K_tar and σ_p0
Here, we are explaining a combinations of parameter K_{\text{mem}}, tether force parameter K_{\text{tar}} and myogenic stress scale \sigma_{p0} that ensures that the pressuirzed wall stay stable and doesn’t drift downstream under the pulsatile flow.
Question. For which combinations of membrane spring K_\text{mem}, tether K_\text{tar} and myogenic stress scale \sigma_{p0} does the pressurized wall stay stable (no blow-up, no wrinkling, no buckling, uniform inflation) and not drift downstream under the pulsatile flow?
Ratios used





















RatioMeaningK_\text{mem}/K_\text{tar}membrane stiffness relative to the axial anchoring\sigma_{p0}/(K_\text{tar}D_0)myogenic stress scale relative to the anchoringR_\text{mem}=\dfrac{K_\text{mem}}{K_\text{tar}}\Big(\dfrac{\Delta s_0}{D_0}\Big)^2membrane tension modulus K_\text{mem}\Delta s_0\Delta s vs. anchoring per length K_\text{tar}\Delta s/\Delta s_0 × D_0^2
Results

Left: which combinations of K_\text{mem} and K_\text{tar} stay stable (6 s runs). Right: the mean downstream offset of the wall falls as 1/K_\text{tar}, exactly as the force balance predicts.


                  
                  Chosen configuration 
                  
                

K_\text{tar}=2.34\times10^9, K_\text{mem}=1.5\times10^{10}, N_b=512, \Delta t=10^{-4} s, P_\text{set}=2 Pa, \sigma_{p0} calibrated for \varepsilon=0.2 → offset 0.29 µm, wall strain ±0.1 %, D/D_0=1.2001 (prediction 1.2000).


Parameter ranges and what happens outside them
(Flow on with pulsatile amplitude 0.6, P_\text{set}=2 Pa unless stated. Each “outside the range” example changes one parameter of the chosen configuration; runs in Simulation_Results/Blood_vessel_v2/2026-10-17/.)
1. Axial tether K_\text{tar} — range 4.5\times10^{8}\lesssim K_\text{tar}\lesssim 1\times10^{10} µm/s²

What it does: holds each wall node at its target point against the wall shear of the flow.
Too small → downstream drift. The wall slides downstream until the tether carries the shear: offset \approx 6.7\times10^{8}/K_\text{tar} µm (right panel). Above 1 % D_0 (1.5 µm) for K_\text{tar}<4.5\times10^8. Example K_\text{tar}=2.34\times10^7 (run_001): the whole wall shifts ≈ 29 µm and slides between 12 and 45 µm with every pulse. It is a static offset — the wall does not keep creeping — and the wall itself stays intact.

Too large → blow-up. The tether force is explicit, so a too-stiff spring overshoots in one time step and the error grows every step. Measured ceiling at \Delta t=10^{-4} s: stable at 1.0\times10^{10}, blow-up at 1.3\times10^{10} (8.4 ms), 1.7\times10^{10} (4.0 ms), 2.34\times10^{10} (2.4 ms, run_005: the whole wall translates axially, ×2.5 per step). The ceiling is numerical and scales as 1/\Delta t.


2. Membrane spring K_\text{mem} — range K_\text{mem}\gtrsim 6\times10^{9} µm/s² (no upper limit found up to 2.5\times10^{10})

What it does: keeps neighbouring wall nodes at their rest spacing (the stiffness of the wall along its length).
Too small → wrinkling, then buckling. A disturbance starts at the open ends of the wall chain (the periodic junction), travels upstream and grows exponentially; the wall crumples locally (strain > ±15 %), the diameter becomes non-uniform, and finally the vessel kinks sideways and the lumen pressure leaks. K_\text{mem}=4\times10^9 (run_002): strain limit at 5.1 s, kink at 7.4 s. K_\text{mem}=2.5\times10^9 (run_003): 4.0 s and 6.1 s — softer walls fail sooner.

A very stiff axial tether (7.4\times10^9) suppresses the wrinkling down to K_\text{mem}=1.5\times10^9 (6 s runs).
Caveat: near this bound the wall strain was still growing at the end of the 6 s runs (e-folding 0.75–1.4 s), and K_\text{mem}=4\times10^9, classed “wrinkled” at 6 s, buckles at 7.4 s. The bound needs confirmation with ≥ 20–30 s runs.

3. Myogenic stress scale \sigma_{p0} — any value tested (\sigma_{p0}/(K_\text{tar}D_0)=2.7\times10^{-5}–1.5\times10^{-2}, i.e. dilation \varepsilon= 10–35 %)

What it does: balances the transmural pressure; it is calibrated from P_\text{set} and the target dilation \varepsilon.
Effect: it only sets the equilibrium diameter (reached to 10^{-4}); it does not affect stability. Larger dilations strain the wall slightly more.

4. Transmural pressure P_\text{set} — range ≲ 2.5 Pa (tested stable: 1, 2, 2.5 Pa)

Too large → pressure-induced buckling. The wall has no axial tension and no bending stiffness, so the pressure acts like an axial compressive load ≈ P\,D. At 10 Pa (run_004) the vessel inflates normally, then short sideways wrinkles (~12 along the vessel) grow within 0.6 s and it snaps into one large S-bend at 2.1 s. Afterwards the vessel leaves the fixed source band and the pressure control fails (see 05 Forces > 5.5 Lumen pressurization (source/sink)); the later “collapse” is an artifact of the method.
Physiological pressures (5–8 kPa) would need an axial pre-tension or bending stiffness, and a much smaller \Delta t.

5. Numerical parameters

N_b=512 wall nodes (\Delta s_0\approx\Delta x/2). With N_b=200 (\Delta s_0\approx1.3\,\Delta x) the flow excites a node-scale sawtooth that ends in buckling.
\Delta t=10^{-4} s. It sets the K_\text{tar} ceiling (∝ 1/\Delta t) and is needed by the stiff myogenic stress at higher pressures.
Radial tether K_y=9.36\times10^5 (not varied): deliberately weak, so that the radial position is decided by pressure, springs and myogenic stress.

8.3 Inflation and deflation with axial flow
Goal. With the chosen stable configuration (8.2: N_b=512, K_\text{tar}=2.34\times10^9, K_\text{mem}=1.5\times10^{10}) and the pulsatile flow on throughout, inflate the vessel with the transmural pressure and then change (i) the myogenic tone and (ii) the transmural pressure, to see how the vessel dilates and constricts.

(sim = mean D/D_0 over the last 0.4 s of each level; pred = force balance D/D_0=1+\ln\!\big(1+(e^{k_p\varepsilon D_0}-1)/a\big)/(k_pD_0).)


Every level reaches the predicted equilibrium (error ≤ 6×10⁻⁴; the largest errors are for the softest wall, k_p=0.05, which relaxes most slowly within the 1.5 s steps). The response is reversible: back at a=1 the vessel returns to D/D_0=1.200.
k_p sets the sensitivity: between tone 0.5 and 2 the diameter changes by 14 % (k_p=0.05), 8.7 % (k_p=0.1) and 4.6 % (k_p=0.2) of D_0 — a stiffer exponential law resists both dilation and constriction.
Each tone step produces a pressure transient (up to 4 Pa / down to 1 Pa): the massless wall changes its stress instantly, the source then drains or fills the lumen in ≈ 0.3–1 s, faster for larger k_p.

Deflation and re-inflation by the transmural pressure





































PhasePsim D/D_0pred.inflated2 Pa1.20011.2000deflation1 Pa1.15711.1570re-inflation2.5 Pa1.21431.2142back2 Pa1.20011.2000

The vessel follows the pressure to the predicted equilibria; 2.5 Pa is stable with the 512-node wall (with 200 nodes and K_\text{mem}=2.34\times10^9, ≈ 2.5 Pa was already at the buckling threshold).
In this (passive) Eq. 18 law the diameter depends only on the ratio P/(a\,\sigma_{p0}): halving the pressure (1.1571) and doubling the tone (1.1572) give the same diameter. An active myogenic response (tone that rises with pressure, as in Arthurs et al. 1998, Eq. 61) is needed to obtain autoregulation.

09-discussion.title: 09 Discussion
09-discussion.content:
9. Discussion and Known Issues
← 08 Experiments | Next: 10 Next Steps
Uniform vs inlet drive
For driving the flow, the uniform body force is the physically correct choice. In a real vessel the flow is driven by the pressure difference between the two ends, with pressure falling linearly along the axis. A periodic domain cannot hold a net pressure drop; the standard substitute is a uniform body force G=-\partial_x p/\rho, which yields exactly the Poiseuille solution, and the physical pressure is recovered as p_\text{phys}=p_\text{periodic}-\rho Gx.
The former inlet drive (force on 4 columns only) acts like a localized pump:

the entire axial pressure drop is concentrated in a ≈ 23 µm-wide step at the inlet, which loads the nearby wall — no such structure exists in a vessel;
the mean luminal pressure equals the exterior pressure, so the upstream half of the vessel sees positive and the downstream half negative transmural pressure. Real vessels never carry negative transmural pressure; in the simulations this produced bulging near the inlet and collapse downstream.

What actually loads a vessel wall



































LoadReal magnitudeUniform driveInlet driveMean transmural pressure (balanced by wall tension, Laplace’s law)≈ 40–60 mmHg (5–8 kPa)absentabsent (zero mean)Pulse pressure (drives pulsation)several–15 mmHgabsentabsentAxial pressure drop over 1.5 mm~ Pa (≈ 5 Pa in this model)implicit in G, not felt by the wallpresent, as a step with ± halvesWall shear stress≈ 0.2 Pa✓✓
The pressure pulse travels at several m/s, so at 1 Hz its wavelength (metres) is far longer than the 1.5 mm segment: over this segment the pulse is spatially uniform and the real wall breathes in phase along its length. Neither drive reproduces this; it requires a separate transmural-pressure load on the wall (10 Next Steps).
Lumen area is conserved
The walls are (almost) impermeable and the lumen is periodic in x, so fluid cannot enter or leave it; incompressibility then fixes the lumen area. Measured: area constant to 10^{-4} in the baseline run and to 3\times10^{-3} in the other uniform-drive runs. Consequences:

the mean diameter cannot change; only redistributions (one part widens while another narrows) are possible — exactly the anti-phase pattern in 08a Earlier Experiments > A.7 Baseline run (isotropic tether, 5 s);
a physiological, in-phase dilation of the whole segment is impossible in the present set-up. A real segment dilates because during systole more blood enters than leaves. Options: open inflow/outflow boundaries (requires replacing the FFT solver), or allowing exchange with the exterior region.

Origin of the wall motion in the baseline
With the uniform drive the wall feels only shear. The shear drags the interior of the wall downstream against the tethers (static offset ≈ \tau_w/(K_\text{wall}\,\Delta s/\Delta s_0) ≈ 70 µm), and the pulsatile part makes it slide back and forth; the non-uniform sliding produces the ±1 % diameter changes. The wall oscillation is therefore a by-product of axial motion, not a radial pulsation.
Trade-off seen in the mapping study: K_\text{wall} ×10 reduces the offset to 0.05 D_0 but also reduces the diameter oscillation by ~50× — the wall becomes effectively rigid.
Compressive collapse and the anisotropic tether

With the isotropic tether, the axial sliding that produced the wall oscillation also compressed the downstream half of the wall (≈ −9 %). A spring chain with no bending stiffness is unstable in compression; one segment shortens a little every cycle until nodes overlap (08a Earlier Experiments > A.8 Long-run compressive collapse (isotropic tether)). Larger pulse amplitudes collapse sooner.
It is a mechanical, not a numerical instability: refining the wall to \Delta s\approx\Delta x/2 did not help; spring pre-tension only delays it.
Separating the tether into a strong axial and a weak radial part removes the cause: the wall is held lengthwise (as perivascular tissue does in vivo) and stays in its stable, slightly stretched state, while radially it is nearly free (08a Earlier Experiments > A.9 Anisotropic tether).
The price is that, with a purely axial load (uniform drive), the wall now hardly moves at all. Visible, physically meaningful deformation must come from a radial load — the transmural pressure (10 Next Steps).
Remaining artifact: the two end segments at the periodic junction carry a constant +12 % / −9 % strain because the interior shifts ≈ 6 µm as a whole while the ends are pinned. A closed (periodic) spring chain with uniform tethering would remove it.

Effective channel width
The 4-point delta function smears each wall over ≈ 2 grid cells, so the no-slip surface is not exactly at y=y_b,y_t. The simulated peak velocity is 7 % below Poiseuille, which corresponds to an effective width H_\text{eff}\approx0.966\,D_0, i.e. ≈ 1 grid cell narrower. This is a known IB effect; for quantitative WSS it should be calibrated (or the grid refined).
Exterior backflow
The exterior fluid moves with a small uniform velocity (≈ −0.1 to −0.2 mm/s) opposite to the lumen flow. In a fully periodic domain the total momentum is set by the balance of the drive and the tether forces; the uniform (zero-wavenumber) velocity mode is not damped by viscosity. Likely harmless for the wall dynamics but should be checked (e.g. by monitoring the domain-mean velocity).
dtheta vs node spacing

The spreading weight dtheta =L_y/N_b=2.5 µm is inherited from the circle-in-flow code; the actual node spacing is \Delta s_0=7.54 µm.
Decision (2026-10-11): kept as is; the factor 2.5/7.54\approx0.33 is absorbed into the effective stiffnesses (and taken into account in the March → physical mapping). Effective physical values are K\cdot\texttt{dtheta}/\Delta s_0 for density-type forces.
Related: the spring force is computed as a nodal force while tether and myogenic forces are force densities, yet all are spread with the same weight.
Node spacing \Delta s_0\approx1.3\Delta x is larger than the usual IB guideline (\Delta s\lesssim\Delta x/2); the measured area conservation shows no significant leakage at current loads, but leakage appeared under the large inlet-drive loads (area +3 %).

Spring force without pre-tension
Rest length = initial spacing → a straight wall has zero tension and the springs give no transverse stiffness. All radial restoring force comes from the tethers (and myogenic stress when on). Evidence: identical results for K_\text{mem}=4\ldots200 in Phase B. A pre-tension (rest length < spacing) would add a curvature-dependent restoring force T\kappa, closer to a real membrane.
Eq. 18

Source: Michele et al. (2006), Eq. 18 (05 Forces > 5.3 Myogenic force (Michele et al. (2006), Eq. 18)); the unit/continuity question below should be checked against that paper.
Branches have inconsistent units and a slope jump at r_0; the compression branch is ~50× softer near r_0.
Once a transmural pressure is modelled, Eq. 18 becomes the natural counter-force; its parameters should then be chosen so that \sigma_p balances the mean transmural pressure at the target diameter.

Model limitations

2D planar geometry: no hoop stress; “diameter” is the gap between two plates.
Myogenic pairing by node index assumes horizontal walls without relative sliding — violated once the walls drift.
Force evaluation mixes \mathbf X^n (spring, myogenic) and \mathbf X^{n+1/2} (tether).
Laplacian/CN factor use \Delta x for both directions (0.4 % mismatch with \Delta y).

Pressure-induced buckling of the pressurized vessel

Above ≈ 2–4 Pa (with the current stiffnesses) the pressurized vessel first develops a local pinch and then kinks sideways (08a Earlier Experiments > A.11 Pressurized lumen and myogenic stimulation (2026-10-13)). Halving \Delta t or refining the wall does not change it, so it is a property of the model, not of the numerics.
This is the classic buckling of a pressurized tube that is held axially but carries no axial tension: when the tube bends, the internal pressure acting on the inner and outer side of the bend gives a net sideways force ∝ P\,D\,\kappa, i.e. the pressure acts like an axial compressive load \approx P D. Real arteries are stabilized by their in-vivo axial pre-stretch (axial tension larger than this load); when that tension is lost they become tortuous.
In the model the walls have no tension (springs without pre-tension) and no effective bending rigidity, so the only resistance is the axial anchoring — consistent with the observation that stiffer axial anchoring raises the critical pressure (2.5 → 7 → ≈ 10 Pa).
Stabilizing physiological pressures (5–8 kPa ≈ 1000× larger) would need an axial wall tension of order PD and/or a real bending stiffness; with the explicit IB coupling this forces \Delta t down to ~10^{-6} s or below. Options: (i) wall pre-tension as a constant tension term (no extra stretch stiffness), (ii) a centerline tether that resists lateral displacement without resisting dilation, (iii) a semi-implicit IB time step. Until then, pressures of a few Pa are used and results are interpreted through the force balance (which is linear in P for a calibrated \sigma_{p0}).

IB wall permeability under pressure

An IB wall is slightly permeable at the grid scale: with a pressure jump across it, a small steady flow leaks through. With R_\text{src}=1.3\times10^5 the leak held P_\text{lumen} at 4.3 Pa instead of 10 Pa (estimated leak resistance ≈ 10^5 s⁻¹). With R_\text{src}=2\times10^4 the source compensates and P_\text{lumen} stays at P_\text{set} to 0.1 %.

Wall discretization under flow (200 vs 512 nodes)

With N_b=200 (\Delta s_0=7.5 µm \approx1.3\,\Delta x) the pulsatile flow excited a node-scale axial sawtooth of the pressurized wall (neighbouring nodes moving in opposite directions, ≈ 1.2 µm), independent of \Delta t, which ended in sideways buckling after a few seconds (08a Earlier Experiments > A.11 Pressurized lumen and myogenic stimulation (2026-10-13)).
With N_b=512 (\Delta s_0\approx\Delta x/2, the usual IB guideline) and a stiff enough membrane (K_\text{mem}\gtrsim6\times10^9) the sawtooth is gone (0.004 µm) and the vessel stays stable under flow at 2–2.5 Pa (08 Experiments > 8.3 Inflation and deflation with axial flow). A plausible reason: with \Delta s_0>\Delta x the nodes sample the near-wall shear at different positions relative to the grid (an aliasing pattern of wavelength \Delta x\Delta s_0/|\Delta s_0-\Delta x|\approx26 µm, the same scale as the instability seen earlier), which disappears when \Delta s_0 divides \Delta x.
The stable window of 08 Experiments > 8.2 Stable parameter range for K_mem, K_tar and σ_p0 has a simple structure: the tether must carry the wall shear (lower bound, offset =\tau_w/(K_\text{tar}\Delta s/\Delta s_0)) but stay below the explicit time-step limit (upper bound); the membrane must be stiff enough to keep the nodes evenly spaced against the flow (lower bound), and no upper bound appeared; \sigma_{p0} only sets the dilation.

index.title: IBM Arteriole Wall Simulation — Report (Blood_vessel_v2)
index.content:
2D Immersed Boundary Simulation of an Arteriole Wall


                  
                  Abstract 
                  
                

We model a straight segment of a small cerebral artery (D_0 = 150\ \mum, L = 1.5 mm) as two elastic walls immersed in blood, using a 2D penalty immersed boundary method with an FFT-based Navier–Stokes solver in physical units (\nu = 3.3\times10^{-6} m²/s). The walls are held by uniform tethers (stiff along the wall, weak across it) and membrane springs; a myogenic passive-stress law is implemented but currently switched off. Flow is driven by a uniform, time-modulated body force that stands in for a pulsatile pressure gradient (u_\max \approx 2.5 mm/s, Re \approx 0.11, Womersley \alpha\approx0.1).
The project goal at this stage is a parameter set for which the wall oscillates regularly without numerical blow-up. Starting from a stable March 2026 configuration (non-physical code units), we derived a load-to-stiffness mapping to physical scale (K_\text{phys} = 9.36\times10^5\,K_\text{March}). The mapped parameters give periodic wall motion (diameter oscillation ≈ 2 %) and reproduce plane Poiseuille flow to within 7 %, but longer runs reveal a compressive collapse of the wall: the mean shear drags the wall downstream against its pinned ends. An anisotropic tether (strong axially, weak radially) removes the collapse and leaves the wall free to move radially; with the present uniform drive, however, nothing loads the wall radially and the closed periodic lumen conserves its area, so the wall barely moves. The next step is a pressure-controlled source/sink (as in Arthurs et al., 1998) to pressurize the lumen, so that dilation and constriction can be studied through the myogenic stress.


Contents
